michaelfromUS12
Just as good as the first.This is a story about Paul and his mother Jessica achieving greatness. Paul starts off as a happy youngling, living in bliss under his father, then he becomes a more serious man and a leader due to House politics. A young but capable Paul then leads a severely depleted House Atredies with his dutiful mother governing the rank and file behind the veil. Jessica leads the people in culture and spirituality while rallying support for her son, ensuring their survival. Bene Gesserit powers are present and used frequently by her. Jessica's story is especially satisfying. We see Paul and Jessica come into their natural positions as leaders of a ruined House and attempt to restore it to glory. This all leads to a culmination of Great House politics, and House Atredies overcoming and surpassing those that sought to destroy them.I love Paul, Jessica and Leto. I'm glad the story focuses on that family and the actors they picked to represent them are well chosen. The Sand Worms are more prominently shown in this film, with them being more actively used in human politics and culture. This is a good thing, as spice and the worms that create it are the single pillar Dune culture everywhere in the galaxy rests on.

ClownNiko
Denis Villeneuve's second film adaptation of Frank Herbert's Dune series is a visually stunning science fiction masterpiece that thoroughly entertains the viewer. The cast and their performances, along with Hans Zimmer's score, make the film a truly memorable experience. However, it must be said that the story and its intricate web of relationships between different races can sometimes be difficult to follow. The narrative itself, unfortunately, no longer offers anything new. This was likely different when the novels were first published in the 1960s. Today, it evokes similar stories from Star Wars and Lord of the Rings. Here, too, the themes are imperial power, war, oppression, and the rebellion of the supposedly weaker. Nevertheless, Denis Villeneuve has succeeded in bringing the material to life in the best possible way, creating a truly great cinematic experience.

famfacat
A Millennia-Spanning Salvation Saga Proving the Power of the Heart Outshines Mere Force, Elevated by an Exceptional Cast and Deep Narrative Flavor.240614 (4.0)Unlike the slightly sluggish pace of Part 1 which had to set up the vast worldbuilding, this sequel is thoroughly flavorful and engaging. The casting is outstanding, and while I previously held a mild aversion toward Timothée Chalamet feeling he always played similar roles, his sincere and intense performance completely won me over. The opening narration featuring the magnetic voice of Florence Pugh as Princess Irulan immediately sets an incredible tone. Emperor Shaddam IV, who once treasured Duke Leto Atreides like a son, is left hollow and grief-stricken after following the dictates of the Spacing Guild to leave Leto to his demise. The depiction of Baron Vladimir Harkonnen feels distinctly predatory, and his sinister fixation on his nephew Feyd-Rautha goes far beyond mere jealousy. A pregnant Lady Jessica displays immense presence, piercing through high-tech Harkonnen confinement with sheer force and raw instinct. In the deep desert where moisture is sacred, the Fremen conserve every drop, recycling their own bodily fluids through stillsuits and meticulously extracting water from the deceased to store in sacred underground basins, treating even tears with extreme reverence. Stilgar offers the dying Reverend Mother's mantle to Jessica. To sit in the seat of ancestral wisdom, she must ingest the Water of Life—a fatal poison to men—which is extracted by drowning a young sandworm. As an advanced Bene Gesserit adept at transmuting toxins, Jessica drinks the liquid alongside her unborn child, causing the old Reverend Mother to pass away. The Fremen are culturally divided: northern fundamentalists lean skeptical of the messianic myths, while the southern communities deeply embrace the prophecy of the savior, leading Chani to initially scoff at the dogma while Stilgar zealously champions Paul as the Lisan al-Gaib. In Jessica's womb, the unborn Alia already communicates telepathically, guiding Paul on how to become the ultimate warrior. The greedy Harkonnens relentlessly exploit Arrakis, pushing into the uninhabitable, worm-infested deep desert reminiscent of the Naga invading the harsh northern lands in the novel "The Bird That Drinks Tears". In response, Paul marches alongside the Fremen, gradually becoming their true liberator while vowing to fight for their freedom rather than personal vengeance, earning the honorable secret name Usul. When Paul humbly requests Muad'Dib as his warrior name—referencing the small, resilient desert mouse rather than a shadow on the second moon—Stilgar embraces it with reverence, praising the creature for its profound wisdom in creating its own moisture and pointing the way forward. The traditional naming ritual, where each clan member embraces Paul while calling his new name, feels wonderfully authentic. Chani's secret name, Sihaya, means the desert spring of prophecy. Learning to summon and ride the colossal Shai-Hulud requires painstaking technique and profound trust earned through Stilgar's mentorship. As a prescient leader, Paul's glimpses into the future grant him resolve, knowing what dangers will not claim his life. Jessica travels to the skeptical northern regions to proselytize, demonstrating her political brilliance by uniting the Fremen under religious fervor. The film thoughtfully avoids gratuitous romantic melodrama. Reminiscent of Duke Leto's political calculations, Alia advises keeping the most crucial strategic seat open for a royal alliance, effectively relegating Chani to a concubine. Beast Rabban loses control of the capital to Muad'Dib's relentless guerilla tactics and flees in panic. Princess Irulan, a sharp pupil of the Bene Gesserit, astutely warns the Emperor that the religious devotion surrounding Muad'Dib is far more formidable than imperial military might, suspecting that this desert leader is Paul. Feyd-Rautha is portrayed as a bloodthirsty, sociopathic duelist who slaughters his own servants to test blade edges; the Baron promises him the throne of Arrakis upon quelling the rebellion. Léa Seydoux appears as Lady Margot Fenring, a Bene Gesserit operative who tests Feyd-Rautha as a potential messianic bloodline candidate and secures his child to preserve the selective genetic line. Paul reunites with Gurney Halleck and his surviving soldiers, who stayed behind in the desert to avenge Duke Leto by hunting Rabban; Gurney leads Paul to the Atreides family's hidden nuclear arsenal. Hesitant to trigger a devastating galaxy-wide holy war that he foresees if he travels south, Paul grapples with the terrifying burden of his destiny. He eventually drinks the Water of Life to pierce through the past and see the future, awakening fully as the Kwisatz Haderach with the help of Chani's tears acting as the prophesied spring. Alia is revealed to be portrayed by Anya Taylor-Joy in a striking vision.

CarmaWarlock
It's weird how this movie has so many fewer reviews than the first one. I smell Metacritic shenanigans to bump the score up higher than the first one. Dune 1 established the style which is the most striking accomplishment of the series. Yes the narrative feels unfinished but that's to be expected; it's the first half of a single novel. Dune 2 carries all of that forward while having the benefit of resolution which adds to the satisfaction factor. However this film rewrites the novel in ways that are unforgivable. In an attempt to modernize the narrative (or whatever, I just see it as feminist propaganda) they completely ruin Channi's arc in an attempt to make her seem less dependent and more strong and independent. In chasing trends it actually makes the character seem petty. There's real strength in the novel and a sense of yearning in Chani's decision to accept her role as Paul's crypto love interest playing second fiddle to a union that is overall better for the power structure. These decisions at the stake of this narrative feel more real than a love interest attempting to call the shots with a god-king. It's like Dune was rewritten as a YA novel. Really disappointing stuff, although I'm sure the producers insisted the changes be made like they always do.

My mind is reeling. That was one of the best films I have ever seen. Dune: Part Two is one of the best sequels I have ever seen. High in the ranks with Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse, The Dark Knight, Captain America: The Winter Soldier, and The Hunger Games: Catching Fire, it stands strong in the center of a story, where other second installments have failed. The film picks up right after the ending of Dune: Part One. It feels as though the last 2 years and 4 months (the 2021 October release of Dune: Part One) have only passed in the blink of an eye. Dune: Part Two is crafted with precisely the same skill, passion, and creativity that Denis Villanueve and his team brought to Dune: Part One. It is impossible to select a favorite as they are just what they are titled - two parts of the same story. Watch Part One before going to see Part Two, and you’ll walk away thinking it was a single 6-hour film. Seamless. The first act of Dune: Part Two is noticeably slower-paced than the first movie, so at first it's concerning as a potential indicator for the rest of the film. This first hour-and-a-half is dedicated to the development of the characters and important plot points and is interesting enough to keep you engaged. This section of the storyline climaxes with Paul riding the sandworm. The scene is astounding, powerful, jaw-dropping… it is the high point of Paul’s character development arc. In this video, 'Dune: Part Two' Director Denis Villeneuve Breaks Down a Scene | Vanity Fair, Villanueve shares the vision and production magic behind this scene. Just when you're wondering when something terrible will happen, Feyd-Rautha Harkonnen steps onto the screen. The middle of the film is dominated by the gladiator arena scene, shot in infrared black and white. This brilliant cinematography choice amplifies the contrast of the pale Harkonnens against their black war paint. It's more than enough to set you on edge and show you that Feyd-Rautha is a formidable enemy. CONTINUE READING ON LETTERBOXD: ****/62xgJD

DiegoMesa10
Dune Part Two shines with its stunning cinematography, immersing viewers in the world of Arrakis. Roger Deakins and Denis Villeneuve craft a visually striking and emotionally potent portrayal of the desert planet, making the audience feel deeply connected to the Fremen's world. Particularly impressive are the sequences depicting the Fremen riding sandworms, which are both thrilling and beautifully executed.Chani, portrayed by Zendaya, has a much more prominent role in this film compared to the first. Her character adds depth to the story, particularly in exploring the Fremen’s skepticism of Paul Atreides as their Messiah. Her evolving belief in Paul and recognition of his transformation into something otherworldly provide compelling layers to her character and their **** performances are stellar across the board. Florence Pugh as Princess Irulan, Christopher Walken as the Emperor, and Austin Butler as Feyd-Rautha deliver memorable portrayals, with Butler standing out despite some media overhype. Returning cast members, including Timothée Chalamet and Rebecca Ferguson, also shine, especially in showcasing the evolution of Paul and Lady Jessica. Their transformations into powerful, almost alien figures are fascinating, though at times **** ending, while exciting, felt slightly incomplete. Chani’s departure and the final sandworm scene left the reviewer intrigued but yearning for more closure. However, this anticipation heightens excitement for the third installment.Overall, Dune Part Two successfully continues the saga, blending stunning visuals, strong performances, and a nuanced narrative. Despite minor critiques, the film leaves audiences eagerly awaiting the next chapter.

Director, Denis Villeneuve, proves once again that he can tell a beautiful-looking incoherent story and that shoving a bunch of A list celebrities in one film can still result in a muddled mess of bad acting. True, Dune 2 does pay off the extremely disappointing and pointless ending of the first film, but Denis’ inability to create or flesh out characters was really the downfall of the film and there is no better example than this than Christopher Walkin, who Denis tries to make the Star wars Empire strikes back Emperor. Unfortunately, Walken is given so little characterization that he just comes off as the loveable funny character he is in all of his films, which does not work and comes off more like a joke. Dave Butista’s character in this film is just yelling. By far his worst acting in any film. Denis struggles to even keep poor Timothee Chalamet’s character consistent as one second he is so deeply in love with Zendaya, and then randomly ditches her for a declared future political marriage that is rejected by all of the houses a mere two minutes after it happens yet he still goes through with it. Perhaps this also happens in the book but Denis is just so bad at story telling that the audience is still reeling over the fact that there was an emperor in Dune as poor Denis forgot to show that he existed in the first film. Instead he pads the movie again with repeat ‘visions’, because Denis has the story telling skills of manga fan artist. Florence Pugh, who is a great actress, is forbidden from emoting or showing any character at all, forcing another talented actor to have bad acting. The people who like this movie are the same people who are awed by Michael Bay movies, but at least Bay can make action. Denis seems to think all fights must contain a roll dodge that goes into a kick, since he reuses this move in almost every fight scene of the movie, multiple times. Denis should stick to concept designs and stay away from the director’s chair. I now know three people who attempted to watch Dune on a bad airplane screen, and since they couldnt enjoy the only thing Denis is good at, visuals, got bored and turned off the film.

Un blockbuster muy bien hecho, a la altura de las obras literarias. Música, sonido y fotografía son las partes más impresionantes; aunque falla un poco en el desarrollo de los nuevos antagonistas. Espero la tercera parte con ansias.
